newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Few big EMU decisions face Dutch EU presidency.
newsitem.headline: Few big EMU decisions face Dutch EU presidency.

text.p: Reflecting the significant progress already made towards economic and monetary union (EMU), the new Dutch EU presidency has all but admitted there is little to do on the single currency over the next six months.

In briefings this week in The Hague and in a letter to his European Union counterparts, Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm said the outgoing Irish presidency had dealt with all the major decisions facing the bloc for now.
"A lot of the important work has already been done," Zalm said in the letter, which outlined his agenda for so-called ECOFIN meetings, the monthly get-togethers of EU finance and economy ministers.
The Netherlands took over the EU presidency on January 1 from the Irish, who successfully steered the bloc through a number of EMU-related minefields.
In what was hailed as a breakthough for the single currency, EU leaders at their summit in Dublin in December agreed a pact to ensure budgetary discipline after the euro is introduced.

It includes fines for running excessive deficits and lays out the circumstances in which they will be imposed. The EU leaders also agreed on a legal framework for the euro and on an exchange-rate mechanism for EU countries outside the euro zone.
Zalm, who had high praise for Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn's shepherding of the potentially explosive issues, said what he was left with was the task of building on the decisions.
With the political decisions out of the way, much of the work will be technical, including drafting the regulations both for the legal framework and for the budgetary pact.
The ministers will also set about drafting a formal resolution on creating a post-EMU exchange rate mechanism.
This will have to be adopted by EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam in June. But again, the political decision has already been made, meaning that what is agreed will likely get a rubber stamp.
A European Commission official said the emphasis on preparing for the euro had now shifted from EU institutions to companies, banks and others who would have to do business under the new regime.

"It may be that ECOFIN meetings will be less dominated by strategic EMU thinking, but that is because essentially the architecture has been agreed," the official said. "Now we shift to the private sector to respond."
Zalm, meanwhile, has told his colleagues he expects ECOFIN meetings to focus on employment issues, on combatting fraud and on various tax and finance services issues.

The ministers will get to see proposed new euro coins at an informal meeting in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, in April. The notes, unveiled at the Dublin summit, got mixed reviews but were seen as underlining the fact that the euro was on its way.
